text:
Sprites and ELVES
Although we are most familiar with the white, branching lightning caused by electrical discharge between clouds and the ground, there are many types of lightning. This fortuitous image captures two: tentacled red sprites and ring-like ELVES. Sprites extend upward from the top of a thunderstorm, in a large but weak flash that lasts only seconds. ELVES appear as a rapidly-expanding disc, thought to be caused by an energetic electromagnetic pulse moving into the ionosphere. They were first discovered in footage from a 1992 Space Shuttle mission. (Image credit: V. Binotto; via APOD)

Mais, si vous êtes d’accord, comprenez-vous que nous risquons d’échouer ? Il faut bien comprendre le prix à payer, la réalité de nos vies. Parfois nous partons, nous nous échinons, nous souffrons et, malgré tout, nous n’apprenons rien. Nous sommes fragiles. Est-ce nous que vous voulez là-haut ? Préféreriez-vous des machines limitées mais prévisibles ? Ou bien la flexibilité de l’intelligence humaine vaut-elle de peut-être briser nos corps et nos esprits ? »Il y a dans cette citation d’Apprendre, si par bonheur quelque chose comme le cœur battant de la pensée de Becky Chambers : une profession de foi limpide, presque fragile, portée par la conviction que la connaissance, même dénuée d’utilité immédiate, demeure l’un des plus nobles accomplissements humains.Ces mots rappellent que l’exploration n’est ni conquête ni promesse de richesse ; elle est un pari risqué sur notre propre vulnérabilité. Gemini and Context Splicing
Reading Time:   3 minutesImagine that you're out for a walk. You're looking at the landscape and taking photos with your camera or phone. At the same time your GPS watch, or phone app is recording your location every second. What remains of the walk is a gps track that has a resolution of one set of gps co-ordinates per second, and photos when you took photos. Most of the walk is "lost" because to record video of the entire walk would be too consuming.To use another image. For many years podcasters would record one and a half hours of show, but they would edit it, keeping just the best thirty minutes. In the case of the blurb to describe a podcast you might have three to five sentences, chapter markers, and possibly a list of hyperlinks.Trying to Remember a ConversationAI, too, has a limited attention span. In theory Gemini can accept up to a million tokens but in practice it is quite a bit lower. A token is a snippet or phrase of context. The chattier you are, the more snippets of conversation AI models like Gemini need to understand.If you're verbose, and Gemini is, then that's a lot of conversation to remember. We forget, and so does the AI model. It starts to mis-remember things.Context SwitchingLLMs have a huge set of data from which to work, so I expect them to see a screengrab from Immich or Photoprism, and to remember which is which. If I tell it "I'm using the laptop for this, and the Pi for that, I expect it to remember and to automatically switch between the two without me telling it. The issue is that it doesn't. You need to say "I'm using the Pi for this" and "I'm using the laptop for that". It doesn't remember the context, especially with longer tasks.The Gemini TrapIf you're sorting through tens of thousands of files, and you're getting the output from exiftool or other, you're easily coming out with documents with 7 million tokens, but the context window is a million tokens. Gemini doesn't say "Wait, I can't handle such a large data set". It hallucinates instead.Helping GeminiWhen I noticed this I started a new chat. I also asked Gemini, How can I provide you with enough data for you to understand it, without being overwhelmed so it said give me the head and the tail (paraphrased) and I'll draw conclusions from that. From that moment on I tried to give Gemini enough for it to understand the output, without giving it excess information.Grep and Other CommandsIf you have a large data set, instead of feeding it to Gemini as is, you can ask it to help you summarise the data via GREP and other commands. Instead of feeding it a list of jdupes duplicates tell it We have 1200 lines from Source A and 1400 from Source B, and wait for Gemini to provide you with its "thoughts". On the OthersGoogle AI Studio, Le Chat, MyAI and Euria will all say "I'm full" and encourage you either to come back later, or to open a new window. Gemini is like the person in the restaurant in a Monty Python sketch that has another bite and explodes.And FinallyOne of the reasons I like Gemini over other models is that it's patient. It will accept a lot of information. The drawback is that it will start hallucinating before saying "i'm full, I need a break". If you're not cautious it can provide you with the wrong command. That can have serious consequences if you don't dry run and check every command before taking away the safety wheels.In summary, watch for signs of context splicing, and when you spot them get a summary, and move to a new chat and continue from there. I don't know how other AI solutions behave.

text:
Yggdrasil Linux/GNU/X (Alpha 1992) on 86Box with i486 [1992]
Yggdrasil Linux/GNU/X is the first Linux distribution that came up with the concept of the live distribution that came in a single CD-ROM disk. It was named “Plug and Play Linx”, which means that this distro automatically configures itself for hardware.In this article, we will be testing the alpha release of Yggdrasil Linux/GNU/X that was released on December 1992 with the pre-installed Bochs virtual machine ZIP file while integrating its disk image with 86Box. You can find this archive file here.First, we have configured 86Box as follows:The virtual machine has been configured as follows:Machine type: [1992] i486 (Miscellaneous)Machine: [STPC Client] ITOX STARCPU: ST STPC DX @ 66 MHzMemory: 32 MBVideo: [ISA] Tseng Labs ET4000AXKeyboard: AT KeyboardMouse: Mouse Systems Serial MouseSound card: [ISA16] Sound Blaster 16Floppy disk controller: Internal deviceHard disk controller 1: Internal deviceNew hard disk: ygg-c.img (needs resize)
C/H/S: 914/16/63Size: 449 MBBus: IDEChannel: 0:0Floppy drive 1: 3.5″ 1.44MWe have taken the ygg-c.img file from the Bochs virtual machine dump that was apparently made in 2004. Since Bochs 3.0 didn’t work with this virtual machine according to our tests due to deprecated entries and other errors, we have adapted it to 86Box.We’ve started the virtual machine, and let the BIOS automatically detect the drive from the BIOS setup. Afterwards, we’ve let the Yggdrasil Linux distribution start up.This version of Yggdrasil was using Linux version 0.98. Since the initial snapshot of the disk image was made, we’ve configured the X386 server to use our configured virtual machine’s graphics card and the mouse.We’ve launched the vi /usr/lib/X11/Xconfig command to edit the X server configuration file, which showed us the full settings that was generated for the Bochs virtual machine. We need to adapt it to the current configuration of the virtual machine.First, we’ve removed the comment sign, #, from the MouseSystems property, which means that the X server assumes that the Mouse Systems serial mouse has been installed under /dev/ttys1.After that, we went to the vga256 section that specified no configuration for the graphics chipset, which explained why the X server refused to start. We’ve removed the comment sign from the Chipset property that had a value of et4000, which is the chipset for the Tseng Labs ET4000AX that we’ve selected.Afterwards, we’ve started the X server with startx, and we’re greeted with TWM with three terminals and one xclock window. The third xterm and the xclock window were both off-screen due to the virtual resolution of 1024×1024 as “Virtual 1024 1024” specifies.The keyboard works fine, but the mouse cursor moves sluggishly. We’ve examined what X11 applications are currently installed by running ls /usr/X11/bin, and we got the below list.For example, we ran the maze program, and it showed us the randomly generated maze with the X logo being placed.That is one exciting thing to have seen what the oldest Linux distribution in its oldest version looks like. Stay tuned and feel free to follow us for more old operating systems being run on 86Box.

text:
From noise, all this
A new paper has appeared on arXiv: Generative deep learning improves reconstruction of global historical climate records. It uses, as you might guess from the title, generative deep learning to reconstruct global historical climate records. It does temperature and precipitation, but I’m largely interested in temperature.This is a good thing to try becauseit hasn’t been tried before and if anything can recreate the patterns, non-linearities, and grunge of  the real world it’s probably something like this. this is one of the few spatio-temporal models I’ve seen applied to the reconstruction of global temperature so they gain from temporal as well as spatial correlations.it works at 5degree resolution (like HadCRUT) and 1 degree resolution (like Berkeley Earth) or a combo of the two.Their method even gives them uncertainties.This is quite the list.Some of their justification for going the deep learning route is, perhaps a little unfair to existing methods. We know that the best estimate kriged solution is too smooth in data voids, but samples drawn from the posterior go some way to mitigating that. It’s also a feature (not a bug) that kriged1 reconstructions aren’t exact in the sense that they pass exactly through the observed grid cell values. They don’t do this because we know the gridded values are uncertain. Having said that, the results of kriging are still too smooth (and blobby, can we say that in a scientific context?), so we shouldn’t hold it too much against them.Their diffusion model (DM) is trained on CMIP6 and ERA5 data. They withhold the period 2005-2014 for testing and one whole CMIP run. The method gives globally complete fields, but it’s not clear what variable is used. I assume it is air temperature everywhere (easy to extract from models) and not some combination of airt temperature over land and SST over ocean (which is what the observations are). It doesn’t look like they make use of the observational uncertainties. They say their reconstruction is “uncertainty-aware“, which got me rather excited, but that awareness clearly has dead spots and I presume they use that phrase because they do come up with uncertainty ranges albeit teeny tiny ones at a global scale.Tests are based on unrealistic – model data are missing at random – and less unrealistic – model data are missing as they were historically – synthetic data sets based on the withheld data. They also use a subsampled piece of modern data which is a bit more realistic, but even there the errors in the data won’t be quite as gnarly as they are in the true historic case. Making good test data is hard, so this isn’t a great fault, but we need to take the results of the tests with a pinch of salt.In the examples they have chosen to illustrate the paper with, the reconstruction looks pretty good but there are still some features whose realism we might question.Take this Figure, which is part of Figure 4. What is going on in the Berkeley Earth reconstruction for August 1874? Why a ridge of below average temperatures in the Southern Ocean? It might be a sea ice-related feature, but sea ice isn’t one of the inputs, so how realistic might that be? Presumably sea ice effects sneak in through the training data, but there’s nothing to constrain them except for indirectly via clues in the temperature field during the reconstruction.Indeed, how realistic is there reconstruction of Berkeley Earth when it’s global mean (panel b right) takes a warm leap in 1930 or so and stays warm until the end of the series? They claim that “This divergence likely stems from the “dilution effect” of traditional Kriging-based methods, which homogenize large spatial fields” but HadCRUT is kriged too (after a fashion) and Berkeley Earth’s own reconstruction warms more than HadCRUT5. Based on this, it seems the spread of their reconstructions is larger than the spread of the existing pair of datasets, which rather goes against their claim to have reduced uncertainty. It’s hard to prove you’ve made a decisive improvement in the reconstruction of global temperature, but it is still useful and important to populate the range of available estimated.Their method discovers a large number of lost El Nino events in the period 1890 to 1960, with a particular concentration before 1920. It think this is huge, if true. It would be nice to see these lined up against other ENSO indicators like SOI. Their 1860s period – which is a bad time for reconstructing the Pacific because there are almost no observations there for the whole decade – still largely lacks ENSO variability. Maybe there really was nothing going on then.Figure S12 is illuminating. I’ve chopped out panel b here which shows the reconstructions of two El Nino events. Their reconstructions (labelled Ours) are on the right.They pick two events to look at in more detail: the late 1902 and 1918/19 El Ninos. In both cases, they show how the kriging based methods of HadCRUT and Berkeley Earth look unrealistic (the HadCRUT and Berkeley recons are blobby thanks to their isotropic kriging covariances), and suggest that their reconstruction looks more realistic. And they do, sort of. Certainly the 1902 event looks more like a regular El Nino despite the paucity of input observations2. The 1918/19 event on the other hand is somewhat choppier and a warm feature on the northern side of the warm “bulls tongue3” extending from the central Pacific and heading roughly northeast to the coast of America, is clearly a rogue ship or two (or three). Indeed observational nastiness seems to have really made a mess of their Berkeley-based recon4.It’s easy to pick at these reconstructions and we should take care not to dismiss them because of these problems. All reconstructions have problems and it’s as important part of understanding their value as the strengths.One possible strength of this dataset is that it has an interestingly different Arctic. I’ve always been concerned about the Arctic reconstructions. Most datasets follow the GISTEMP approach and extrapolate land temperature anomalies out over ice covered areas, but what is going on in the Arctic is almost certainly a bit more nuanced than that. The new DM reconstruction has more local detail and looks more like the physically informed ERA5: warming in the summer gets pinned by the freezing point of sea water, for example. However, we must remember that ERA5 was one of its inputs, along with a bunch of other models and what we are seeing up there is perhaps more model based than observation based. Their reconstruction suggests less Arctic Amplification than existing datasets and more subregional variation. Again, it’s a structurally new estimate and its differences force us to think a little more about how to do the job a little better.  They say“The distinct warming patterns in the 1900–1980 and 1981–2024 periods, concentrated in regions of sea-ice retreat and coastal zones, likely reflect a response to positive albedo feedbacks and land-ocean contrasts. However, given the persistent discrepancies among reanalysis, satellite, and infilled records, a definitive ground truth remains elusive; thus, all assessments of Arctic climate evolution warrant cautious interpretation regarding their structural uncertainties.”It would have been interesting to compare it to Bruce Calvert’s HadCRU-MLE which also does interestingly different things around the ice edge. It would also be interesting to compare to DCENT-I which does a more realistic job of infilling but without going down the ML route. Also, NOAA uses neural nets for interpolation now. Their introduction and analysis are, in short, missing some important recent advances in reconstruction of global temperature. They quasi justify this by claiming that HadCRUT and Berkeley are IPCC favourites, but NOAA GlobalTemp was also used by IPCC and the next IPCC report will have a much broader range of datasets to draw on so that’s a pretty hefty omission.Data aren’t yet available for me to play with in more detail.It’s an interesting new reconstruction of global temperature based on modern machine learning methods so it adds a methodologically distinct dimension to our understanding of structural uncertainty. The differences in the Arctic and history of El Nino events are especially interesting, but the extent to which these reflect model biases and known, quantified data errors is something to be explored.I’m also very concerned that their global temperature series based on Berkeley looks the way it does. They might want to look at that more carefully.-fin-As usual with this kind of paper, one has to wonder how hard they tried with their “standard” methods used for comparison. No details are given about how they kriged data, for example. ↩︎It’s interesting to contemplate how much of the “realism” is down to having a temporal component and how much to deep-learning. In my open ocean dataset, I used a kalman filter, slightly asymmetric kriging solution, and a simple ENSO patterns to do a reconstruction and my 1902 El Nino looked a lot more like their Diffusion Model reconstructions than the blobby isotropic kriging solutions. Of course, I had to add those elements one by one and the DM method gives you them for free, as it were. “Unsupervised” is, I believe, the term of art.  ↩︎Bulls tongue is the phrase they use. I’ve always said warm tongue without speculating on what species it might be. Each El Nino is different and people are fond of classifying them into lots of subclasses, so this animal-based nomenclature might be a fruitful addition to the literature. ↩︎It’s there in Berekeley’s own reconstruction. HadCRUT avoids this horror because it uses the error covariances that tell it how the errors correlate. Regular kriging assumes the errors are uncorrelated and DM assumes there are no errors. ↩︎

text:
TAXPAYER WIN: New council bosses claim £15,000 a year saving as Llanelli councillor expenses axed
The move delivers on a key election pledge made by the new administration, which seized control of the council recently.At a meeting of the Full Council, members voted to remove the Attendance Allowance (£30 per meeting), the Mayoral Allowance (£1,500 per annum), and the Deputy Mayoral Allowance (£500 per annum).These payments were introduced in 2022 under the previous Labour administration, then led by Councillor David Darkin.The new administration states that unlike County Councillors, who receive salaries due to the scale and statutory responsibilities of their roles, serving as a Town Councillor has always been a voluntary position.This long-standing principle has defined Llanelli Town Council and its operations for decades, according to the new leadership.The Independent Remuneration Panel for Wales did not mandate these payments, simply giving councils the discretion to introduce payments of up to £30 per meeting if they wished.Independent Council Leader Cllr Sean Rees, who also confirmed he would not be accepting the Leader’s Allowance, hailed the decision.“We have been consistent on this issue,” Cllr Rees said. “For decades, the role of a Councillor at Llanelli Town Council has been recognised and respected as a voluntary public service position.”He added: “We said that we would remove these expenses and we have now delivered this in our first meeting as a new Administration.”Deputy Council Leader Cllr Michael Cranham stated that town councillors’ attendance and additional role-based expenses are “unnecessary, counterproductive and are an unjustifiable cost to the taxpayer.”“At a time when households continue to face sustained financial pressure, this £15,000 annual saving represents a meaningful commitment to respecting every pound of public money and restoring trust in local government,” Cllr Cranham added.The following Councillors voted in favour of removing the expenses: Cllr Sean Rees, Cllr Michael Cranham, Cllr Steve Williams, Cllr Louvain Roberts, Cllr Andrew Bragoli, Cllr Sarah Evans, Cllr Terry Davies, Cllr Lillith Fenris, Cllr John Jones, Cllr Amanda Carter, and Cllr Alan Cameron Williams.Labour Town Councillors who were present at the meeting abstained from the vote, a move that is likely to fuel further political debate in the town.The Council has confirmed that these payments will now cease with immediate effect, marking a significant shift in how Llanelli Town Council operates.The new administration also stated it remains committed to supporting future councillors of all backgrounds through targeted discretionary support, which it claims does not drain the budget like the previous expenses system.

“Bacteria represent the world’s greatest success story”*…
John Ruskin, study of lichen on a piece of brick, ca. 1871 But as Stephen Jay Gould goes on to observe (in his 1996 book, Full House: The Spread of Excellence from Plato to Darwin), “They are today and have always been the modal organisms on earth; they cannot be nuked to oblivion and will outlive us all. This time is their time, not the ‘age of mammals’ as our textbooks chauvinistically proclaim. But their price for such success is permanent relegation to a microworld, and they cannot know the joy and pain of consciousness. We live in a universe of trade-offs; complexity and persistence do not work well as partners.”Still, we (more complex) humans have recognized– and accommodated– bacteria for millennia.  As We Make Money Not Art explains in a review of a recent book– We The Bacteria. Notes Toward Biotic Architecture by architectural historians Beatriz Colomina and Mark Wigley— that’s fascinatingly apparent in the history of architecture…This “alternative history of architecture from the point of view of microbes” compiles the research that led to the exhibition We the Bacteria: Notes Toward Biotic Architecture at the 24th Milan Triennale last year. Curated by Colomina and Wigley, the show investigated how microbial ecosystems relate to spatial design and health inequality.The book argues that microbes have not only built the whole planetary biosphere but they have also been the real architects of our homes and cities throughout the ages.
